title: How surprising is 60 heads?
hook: 60 heads in 100 flips. Is that luck, or a rigged coin? First: how often does luck do it?

knows: a fair coin lands heads half the time
doesNotKnow: that a p-value is not the chance the coin is fair

misconception: "p = 0.03" means a 3% chance the coin is fair (that the result is a fluke).
objective: The learner can say that a p-value is how often pure luck (a fair coin) gives a result at least as extreme, here about 3% for 60+ heads in 100, and that it is not the chance the coin is fair.
keyState: At least 250 seeded batches shown with the marker at 60 and some batches shaded past it.

claims.text: For a fair coin flipped 100 times, the chance of 60 or more heads is 2.8% (about 3%).
claims.source: Exact binomial sum P(X >= 60), X ~ Bin(100, 1/2) = 0.02844 (exactTail() in src/demos/probability/how-surprising-is-sixty/model.ts). For reference P(X >= 62) = 0.0105, P(X >= 58) = 0.0666.

claims.text: The stage's batches are seeded fair-coin runs: after 250 batches, 5 had 60+ heads (2.0%); after 500, 16; after 750, 23; after 1,000, 38 (3.8%).
claims.source: batches() in model.ts, mulberry32 seed 100, untuned (the first seed tried). Over seeds 1-500, the number of 250-batch runs with 60+ heads had middle 95% 2-13 (median 7); 2 of 500 seeds gave 0. The reveal quotes only the counts the learner saw at marker 60.

claims.text: A p-value is how often luck alone, with a coin known to be fair, gives a result at least as extreme as the one seen.
claims.source: Wasserstein & Lazar (2016), The ASA Statement on p-Values, The American Statistician 70(2): 129-133 (principle 2 and the informal definition). The lesson uses the one-sided version (60 or more heads).

claims.text: A p-value is not the chance that the coin is fair; working that out would also need to know how common unfair coins are.
claims.source: Wasserstein & Lazar (2016), principle 2: p-values do not measure the probability that the studied hypothesis is true. The prior-dependence follows from Bayes' rule.

recall.question: A study reports p = 0.04 for a new drug. Which statement is right?
options: There is a 4% chance the drug does nothing
If the drug did nothing, results this extreme would turn up about 4% of the time
The drug works in 96% of patients
recall.why: A p-value assumes a model such as no effect or a fair coin, then asks how often results would be at least this extreme. It does not directly give the probability that the model is true.
